column.text: The Harbour Gazette
Spring number · The light, the boats and the museum
The quay at the evening tide, from the gallery of the light. The museum is the long building at the head of the quay.
The lamp-keepers' record

The lamp-keepers of the northern coast kept a record of every evening they lit the harbour light, and the record grew longer than the harbour itself. Each entry gives the hour, the weather and the ships that passed before midnight. Most nights the third column stayed empty, and the keepers took pride in that.

The oldest keeper claimed that she could tell the season from the smell of the oil alone, and she was seldom wrong. Nobody could say when the first entry was made, only that the ink in it had faded to the color of weak tea. When a storm did come, the entries ran past the margin and onto the back of the page.

Under the lamp room stood a cupboard of spare wicks, glass chimneys and one brass bell that nobody remembered buying. A page of the record was ruled into three columns: the hour, the weather, and a line for anything worth remembering. Visitors who read the record in order noticed that the handwriting changed every few years, while the weather never did.
The winter of the great storm

In the winter of the great storm the record runs to four pages for a single night. The oil came by boat in spring and autumn, and a late boat meant a careful winter. A keeper's daughter wrote the entries for six years when her father's hands failed, and her hand is the clearest in the book.

The tower was painted every third summer, white below and red at the gallery. Visitors were few, and the book of their names fills less than a single page. The ones who came by sea signed with the name of their boat; the ones who came by the coast road signed with the name of their village.
The new light

When the board sent the new lens, it came in eleven crates and a letter of instructions longer than the record of that year. The keepers set it up in a week and lit it on a calm night, and the entry for that night says only that the light could be seen from the church at Ardmore.

The old lamp was kept in the cupboard under the lamp room, beside the brass bell. It was lit once more, on the night the new light failed in a gale, and the entry for that night is the longest in the book: three pages in a hand that grows smaller as it goes.

The record ends when the light was made automatic. The last entry gives the hour, the weather and the ships that passed, as the first one did, and below it a line in the daughter's hand: kept to the end. The book is in the museum at the old customs house, in forty volumes.
The museum

The customs house stood empty for twenty years before the town bought it for a shilling and a promise to keep the roof sound. The promise was kept by a committee of four, who met in the long room on the first floor and argued about the gutters for most of every meeting.

The first things the museum showed were the ones nobody else wanted: a figurehead from a wreck, a chest of customs ledgers, a case of birds' eggs and the record of the lamp-keepers, which the board sent over in a cart when the light was made automatic.

Visitors come in the summer, mostly, by the coast road. They read the guide, look at the figurehead and the eggs, and stand longest at the case with the open volume. The museum keeps a book for their names, as the keepers did, and it has filled eleven volumes since the first.
"Kept to the end." — the last line of the record

Opening hours
The museum opens every day from Easter to the end of September, ten till five, and on Sundays in the winter, two till four.
The old lamp is lit on the night of the gale.

Readers who come to the museum ask most often about the night of the gale, and the keeper who wrote three pages in a shrinking hand. The museum keeps the old lamp beside the book, and lights it once a year, on the night of the gale, for as long as the oil in it lasts.

The harbour itself has changed less than the light. The quay was lengthened twice, and the fish market moved from the quay to a shed on the road, but the boats still come in on the evening tide, and the people of the town still walk out to the end of the quay to watch them.

The schoolmistress opened the crates in the spring, and read the forty volumes in order over the summer. She wrote a short guide to them, which the museum still sells at the door, and she put the volume of the night of the gale in a case of its own.

Visitors come in the summer, mostly, by the coast road. They read the guide, look at the figurehead and the eggs, and stand longest at the case with the open volume. The museum keeps a book for their names, as the keepers did.

In the winter the museum opens on Sundays only, and the committee meets in the long room as before. The gutters were replaced the year the roof was mended, and the committee now argues about the windows, which let in the sound of the sea.

Once a year, on the night of the gale, the committee lights the old lamp in the long room and opens the volume at the first page of that night. Whoever is there reads the three pages aloud, one after another, until the oil runs out.
